RFC 1350 has no encryption and no authentication. Content rather than credentials because the protocol has no login of its own — but network-device configuration backups travel over it and those files carry credentials
RFC 1288 has no encryption. Content rather than metadata: it discloses account names and login times — information about people and not a device advertisement

RFC 9110 over TCP; the RFC 2817 upgrade-to-TLS mechanism was never adopted by browsers. The value describes the port SERVING content; a host measured as redirect-only carries http-redirect: instead and this column cannot express that narrower case
RFC 2595 STLS; implicit TLS is 995
DCE/RPC negotiates packet privacy in band (RPC_C_AUTHN_LEVEL_PKT_PRIVACY); whether a caller asks for it is not observable from the port

NetBIOS name service (RFC 1002) has no encryption and no authentication. Credentials and not metadata: Windows falls back to it for name resolution so a forged answer draws an automatic authentication attempt and yields NetNTLM material
NetBIOS datagram service (RFC 1002) has no encryption. Metadata: browser and workgroup announcements with no authentication chain following them
SMB over the NetBIOS session service; SMB 3.0 can encrypt the session (MS-SMB2) and earlier dialects cannot — the dialect is not observable from the port
RFC 3501 STARTTLS; implicit TLS is 993
SNMPv3 USM adds privacy (RFC 3826) on the same port; v1 and v2c carry the community string and all data in clear

SNMPv3 traps may be encrypted (RFC 3826); v1 and v2c traps are cleartext. Exposure is n/a because the posture is not proven cleartext — were a collector ever to prove v1/v2c here the value would be credentials (the community string travels with every trap)
RFC 4511 StartTLS on the same port (RFC 4513 security considerations); implicit TLS is 636
SMB 3.0 negotiates session encryption (MS-SMB2); SMB1 and SMB2 cannot — the dialect is not observable from the port
BSD rexec sends the password in clear; no encrypted mode exists
BSD rlogin has no encryption; SSH (22) replaced it. The login exchange is readable
BSD rsh has no encryption; SSH (22) replaced it. It also executes a command on the host it authenticates to
RFC 5424 over UDP is cleartext; syslog-over-TLS is RFC 5425 on 6514. Content: log records are operational and personal data and routinely quote credentials logged by mistake

Oracle Native Network Encryption is negotiated in band; TCPS (TLS) is 2484

IANA registers 1522/tcp as ricardo-lm (a licence manager) and Oracle documents two database listeners here. Oracle's installation guide (Oracle Database Component Port Numbers and Protocols) says the Oracle Net listener moves from 1521 to the next available port when 1521 is taken: plain TCP with Native Network Encryption negotiated in band. Oracle Autonomous Database serves TCPS (TLS) on 1522 (About Connecting to an Autonomous Database Instance). Which of the two a listener speaks is not observable from the port
UPnP Simple Service Discovery Protocol has no encryption; it is a discovery broadcast in clear. Metadata: device and service descriptions only

RFC 9289 defines NFS over TLS on the same port and NFSv4 krb5p adds privacy; NFSv3 without either is cleartext. Exposure is n/a because the posture is not proven cleartext — an export proved to be NFSv3 without krb5p would be content (the files themselves)

UPnP device control and eventing over plain HTTP; no encrypted variant is defined. Metadata on a workstation (device and service descriptions) — but the same protocol on a gateway carries Internet Gateway Device control where an unauthenticated caller can add port mappings; the port cannot tell the two apart

Proxy control channel in clear; CONNECT tunnels the payload but the proxy exchange itself is unprotected. Content: every request URL is readable — and where proxy authentication is configured it is Basic so the credential crosses too
Active Directory global catalog in clear; the TLS port is 3269. Credentials: an unsigned simple bind puts the distinguished name and password on the wire
TLS is negotiated through the handshake capability flags; whether it is required is a server setting
The SSLRequest packet upgrades the connection in band; whether it is required is a pg_hba.conf setting
Multicast DNS (RFC 6762) has no encryption. Metadata with the rest of the discovery family — but note that Responder-class tooling poisons mDNS as well as LLMNR

Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (RFC 4795) has no encryption. Credentials and not metadata: it sits in the Windows name-resolution fallback chain so a poisoned answer draws an automatic authentication attempt and yields NetNTLM material
Web Services for Devices over plain HTTP; the TLS variant is 5358 but no working encrypted discovery path exists. Metadata: printer and scanner descriptions
AMQP 0-9-1 has no in-band upgrade; the TLS port is 5671. Credentials: the connection-start handshake carries PLAIN SASL login and the message payloads follow in clear

WinRM over HTTP; Negotiate applies message-level encryption whatever the transport does — so a listener alone is not evidence of cleartext. Defaults are AllowUnencrypted=False on both client and service; Basic authentication is disabled on the SERVICE but ENABLED on the client — the half most readers get backwards. Provisioning and image-building tooling routinely turns both protections off deliberately so the defaults are not a safe assumption on an automation-built host. The TLS variant is 5986

The X11 protocol has no encryption of its own; X traffic is protected only by tunnelling it over SSH. Control: the connection cookie crosses in clear and a client on the display reads the screen and injects input — keystrokes including passwords are readable with it

Classic Redis is cleartext; Redis 6 TLS is conventionally a separate port. Control and not content: CONFIG SET and module loading let a caller act on the host — the AUTH password and all cached data cross in clear as well
HTTP on an alternate port; same posture as 80. Commonly an application server serving content rather than redirecting

IANA registers 8081/tcp as sunproxyadmin (Sun Proxy Admin Service) and not as an HTTP alternate; reading it as HTTP is a product convention. Apache Flink for one binds its REST endpoint and web interface to 8081 by default (rest.port) with TLS off unless security.ssl.rest.enabled is set. So a listener alone is weaker evidence than on 8080; the plaintext check's explicit plain http:// request is what settles it

The classic text and binary protocols have no encryption and no authentication. Content: cached application data — including session tokens where an application caches them and those are credential-equivalent

Intel AMT out-of-band management interface over plain HTTP; the TLS variant is 16993. Control: it owns the machine below the operating system and its administrative credentials cross in clear
Intel AMT serial-over-LAN and storage redirection in clear; the TLS variant is 16995. Same family as 16992 — console and boot-media control below the operating system
